claims.claim: Patches are software and operating-system updates that address security vulnerabilities within a program or product; vendors may also release updates to fix performance bugs or add features.

Users should install updates as soon as possible because attackers exploit known vulnerabilities for months or even years after a fix is available; keeping software up to date is the most effective measure to protect a device.
CISA recommends enabling automatic updates whenever possible so updates install as quickly as possible; when automatic options are unavailable, users should periodically check the vendor's website.
Software updates and installers should be downloaded only from trusted vendor sites; attackers use email links and attachments disguised as legitimate updates to deliver malware.
End-of-life (EOL) software is no longer supported or patched by the vendor, leaving newly discovered vulnerabilities open to exploitation; CISA recommends retiring EOL products.

Package managers such as apt install software from managed repositories and rely on the low-level dpkg tool, which unpacks and configures packages onto the filesystem; the system records installed packages so they can be tracked and removed.

Platform-specific apps are typically distributed and installed through a vendor's app store, whereas a website/web app is accessed by navigating in a browser and does not need to be installed from any app store.

sourceRecords.title: Update Software (Secure Our World)
sourceRecords.notes: Consumer guidance: watch for update notifications, install updates as soon as possible (criminals won't wait), turn on automatic updates so devices install them without user input, and that providers issue updates to 'patch' security weak spots. Read via curl with browser user-agent (site returns 403 to the default fetcher). Supports the automatic-updates, prompt-installation, and 'patch closes security holes' claims.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding Patches and Software Updates
sourceRecords.notes: Defines patches as OS/software updates that address security vulnerabilities; explains attackers target vulnerabilities for months/years after updates ship; manual vs automatic updates; recommends enabling automatic updates and only downloading from trusted vendor sites, not email links/attachments; defines end-of-life (EOL) software and recommends retiring EOL products; states keeping software up to date is the most effective defense. Read via curl with browser user-agent (default fetcher gets 403). Primary Tier A source for the security/patching angle.

sourceRecords.title: The Debian GNU/Linux FAQ, Chapter 8: The Debian package management tools
sourceRecords.provider: Debian Project / Software in the Public Interest
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative explanation that high-level tools (apt, aptitude, synaptic) rely on the low-level dpkg to manage packages; dpkg installs by unpacking and configuring a package onto the filesystem and removes prior versions. Used to ground the package-manager distribution method, the 'installation = files placed + registered/tracked' mechanic, and dependency/clean-removal points. Reference only; prose written fresh.

sourceRecords.title: What is a progressive web app?
sourceRecords.notes: Explains that platform-specific apps are usually distributed and installed via the vendor's app store, while traditional websites/web apps are reached by opening a browser and navigating to a URL, with no need to install from an app store. Grounds the app-store and web-app (no-install) distribution methods. Reference only; no text reproduced.
